head: What changes
The rule, with examples
rows: Words that already change completely also take the past this way

blocks.md:
**-(으)셨어요** is the past tense of -(으)세요. Use it when something the honored person did already happened.

할머니께서 어제 집에 가**세요**. (✕ — sounds like something happening now)

할머니께서 어제 집에 가**셨어요**. (○ — something that happened yesterday)

blocks.h: How to build it — just swap 세요 for 셨어요
blocks.md:
The rule for building -(으)세요 stays the same — you only swap the final **세요** for **셨어요**.

가세요 → 가**셨어요**

앉으세요 → 앉**으셨어요**

드세요 → 드**셨어요** (드시다 changes the same way)

items.tip: Grandma went to the hospital yesterday.
Grandpa ate a meal a while ago.
The teacher was sick last week.

blocks.md:
**Mixing up 세요 and 셨어요 changes the tense.** If there’s a word for a past time like “yesterday,” “a while ago,” or “last week,” it must be 셨어요.

어제 오세요. (✕ — sounds like a command to come now, even though it says “yesterday”)

어제 오**셨어요**. (○)

blocks.meaning: Grandma went to the hospital yesterday.
blocks.why: There’s a past-time word, “어제” (yesterday), so the past honorific -셨어요 is used.

blocks.meaning: Grandpa ate a meal a while ago.
blocks.why: “아까” means “a little while ago” — already past. 드시다 takes 셨어요 the same way.

blocks.q: 읽다 — “할머니께서 지난주에 이 책을 다 ___.” Write the past honorific form.
blocks.why: There’s a batchim ㄱ, so -으셨어요 attaches.
“어제” is a past time word, so the past honorific -셨어요 is correct.

blocks.q: This is about the past, so make the 셨어요 clear as you read it.

head: What changes
The rule, with examples
rows: Words that already change completely still work the same way

blocks.md:
**-(으)십니다** is an honorific used in **more formal settings** than -(으)세요 — news, presentations, announcements, a company’s official occasions.

할머니께서 집에 가**세요**. (everyday conversation)

사장님께서 지금 도착하**십니다**. (a company announcement)

**-습니다/-ㅂ니다 is formal, but it isn’t honorific.** For it to be honorific, -시- has to be there too.

오늘 회의를 시작합니다. (formal: yes, honorific: no — the subject can be anyone)

사장님께서 회의를 시작하**십니다**. (formal: yes, honorific: yes — the subject is someone senior)

items.tip: The boss is in the meeting room right now. — a formal announcement
The department head will arrive shortly.
Sir/Ma’am, what would you like to eat? — formal register, as at a restaurant

blocks.md:
**-시- doesn’t attach to things that aren’t people.** Attaching it to an object produces what’s often called “object honorification” — a mistake, even though it’s common.

주문하신 커피 나오**셨습니다**. (✕ — the coffee isn’t a person)

주문하신 커피 나왔습니다. (○)

blocks.meaning: The department head will arrive shortly.
blocks.why: The subject is 부장님 (someone senior), and this is a formal setting like an announcement, so -십니다 is correct. 도착합니다 isn’t honorific — it works for any subject.

blocks.meaning: What would you like to eat, sir/ma’am?
blocks.why: This is a question in a formal setting like a restaurant, so the question form -십니까 is used.

blocks.q: 앉다 — “이쪽으로 ___.” (announcing to a meeting room, in the formal honorific)
blocks.why: There’s a batchim ㄴ, so -으십니다 attaches.

blocks.q: Which sentence wrongly attaches an honorific to an object?
blocks.why: “이 상품은 품절이십니다” attaches -시- to a product (an object), which is incorrect. “품절입니다” is correct.

blocks.say: 손님 여러분, 잠시 후 열차가 도착합니다. 사장님께서는 지금 회의실에 계십니다.
blocks.q: The first sentence isn’t honorific (a train), the second is (the boss). Bring out that difference as you read.

title.en: 3. Asking and offering — 실래요, 시겠어요, 실 거예요

blocks.h: Honorific offers, questions, and plans at a glance
head: Expression
Meaning and use
Example
rows: offering casually, or asking their preference
offering or asking more politely (restaurants, service)

blocks.md:
Besides -(으)세요?, there are several other ways to ask or offer something to someone senior. You pick one based on the setting.

Casually, among friends → -(으)실래요?

Politely, as at a restaurant or in service → -(으)시겠어요?

When asking about a plan → -(으)실 거예요?

items.tip: Would you like a cup of coffee? — a casual offer
Sir/Ma’am, what would you like? — a polite offer (restaurant)

items.ch: 내일 이 자리에 다시 오실 거예요?
items.tip: Will you come back here tomorrow? — asking about a plan

blocks.md:
**-(으)실래요? asks their preference; -(으)시겠어요? is a notch more polite than that.** With a senior person you don’t know well, or a customer, -(으)시겠어요? is the safer choice.

할머니, 이거 드**실래요**? (someone you’re close to)

손님, 이거 드**시겠어요**? (someone you’re meeting for the first time)

blocks.why: Offering politely to a customer you’re meeting for the first time calls for -시겠어요. -실래요 is for people you’re closer to.

blocks.meaning: Grandma, would you like a cup of coffee?
blocks.why: This is a casual offer to a grandmother you’re close to, so -실래요 is natural.

blocks.q: 가다 — “내일 그 모임에 ___?” Write the honorific for asking about a plan.
blocks.why: This is asking about a future plan, so -실 거예요 is used.

blocks.q: What’s the most natural way to offer food to a customer you’re meeting for the first time?
blocks.why: -시겠어요 is the most polite for someone you’re meeting for the first time. 드실래요 is for a somewhat closer relationship.

blocks.say: 차 한 잔 하실래요? 아니면 커피가 더 좋으세요?
blocks.q: This is an offer, so read it with a soft, rising tone.

title.ko: 4강. 종합 실전 — 때와 자리에 맞게 골라 쓰기
title.en: 4. Putting it together — pick the right form for the moment

blocks.h: The honorific endings covered so far
head: Situation
Ending
Example

blocks.md:
**① Who is this about?** — If it’s someone senior, -(으)시- goes in.

**② When?** — Right now, keep it as is; already happened, add -셨-.

**③ Where, and how formal?** — Everyday conversation: -어요. A formal setting: -ㅂ니다. Offering or asking: -실래요/-시겠어요/-실 거예요.

**Changing only one part sounds off.** Always check both the word that changes completely (밥→진지, 먹다→드시다) and the ending (-세요/-셨어요/-십니다) together.

할아버지께서 밥을 드**셨어요**. (✕ — the noun wasn’t changed)

할아버지께서 진지를 드**셨어요**. (○)

blocks.meaning: The boss is in the office right now (formal).
blocks.why: Assuming a formal setting like news or an announcement, -십니다 is correct.

blocks.meaning: Grandma, would you like to try this?
blocks.why: This is a casual offer, so -실래요 is natural.

blocks.q: Rewrite the basic sentence “어제 밥을 먹었어요” as if it’s about your grandfather, in the past honorific.
blocks.hint: 밥 becomes 진지, 먹다 changes completely to 드시다, and since it already happened yesterday, use -셨어요

blocks.q: Rewrite the basic sentence “회의에 가요” as if it’s about the boss, as a formal announcement.
blocks.hint: This is a formal setting like a company announcement, so use -십니다

blocks.q: Which of these doesn’t fit its situation?
blocks.why: This attaches -시- to a product (an object) — object honorification. “품절입니다” is correct.

blocks.say: 할머니, 어제 병원에 다녀오셨어요? 오늘은 좀 어떠세요?
blocks.q: Two honorifics come one after another here — asking about the past, then the present.
